claim: Neurogenesis occurs in the adult brain in the hippocampal dentate gyrus.
source: Neurogenesis occurs in the adult brain in the hippocampal dentate gyrus, an area that contains neurons which are vulnerable to insults and injury, such as severe seizures.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience supported by extensive literature citations in the introduction.

claim: The dentate gyrus contains neurons which are vulnerable to insults and injury, such as severe seizures.
source: Neurogenesis occurs in the adult brain in the hippocampal dentate gyrus, an area that contains neurons which are vulnerable to insults and injury, such as severe seizures.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on neuronal vulnerability in the dentate gyrus.

claim: Previous studies showed that increasing adult neurogenesis reduced neuronal damage after severe seizures.
source: Previous studies showed that increasing adult neurogenesis reduced neuronal damage after these seizures.
evidence: This claim references prior published work by the authors (Jain et al., 2019).

claim: Neuronal damage after severe seizures is typically followed by chronic life-long seizures (epilepsy).
source: Because the damage typically is followed by chronic life-long seizures (epilepsy), we asked if increasing adult-born neurons would prevent epilepsy.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in epilepsy research and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Adult-born neurons were selectively increased by deleting the pro-apoptotic gene Bax from Nestin-expressing progenitors.
source: Adult-born neurons were selectively increased by deleting the pro-apoptotic gene Bax from Nestin-expressing progenitors.
evidence: This is the experimental method used in the study, supported by prior validation of this approach.

claim: Tamoxifen was administered at 6 weeks of age to conditionally delete Bax in Nestin-CreERT2Baxfl/fl mice.
source: Tamoxifen was administered at 6 weeks of age to conditionally delete Bax in Nestin-CreERT2Baxfl/fl mice.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: Six weeks after tamoxifen administration, severe seizures (status epilepticus; SE) were induced by injection of the convulsant pilocarpine.
source: Six weeks after tamoxifen administration, severe seizures (status epilepticus; SE) were induced by injection of the convulsant pilocarpine.
evidence: This describes the experimental timeline and methods.

claim: Mice with increased adult-born neurons exhibited fewer chronic seizures.
source: Mice with increased adult-born neurons exhibited fewer chronic seizures.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by quantitative EEG data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Postictal depression was reduced in mice with increased adult-born neurons.
source: Postictal depression was reduced also.
evidence: This finding is supported by EEG analysis data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The protective effects were primarily in female mice.
source: These results were primarily in female mice, possibly because they were more affected by Bax deletion than males, consistent with sex differences in Bax.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analyses showing significant effects in females but not males.

claim: Female mice were more affected by Bax deletion than males, consistent with sex differences in Bax.
source: These results were primarily in female mice, possibly because they were more affected by Bax deletion than males, consistent with sex differences in Bax.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed sex differences and prior literature on Bax.

claim: Female mice with enhanced adult-born neurons showed less neuronal loss of hilar mossy cells than wild-type females or males.
source: The female mice with enhanced adult-born neurons also showed less neuronal loss of hilar mossy cells and hilar somatostatin-expressing neurons than wild-type females or males, which is notable because loss of these two hilar cell types is implicated in epileptogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical quantification data in Figure 7.

claim: Female mice with enhanced adult-born neurons showed less neuronal loss of hilar somatostatin-expressing neurons than wild-type females or males.
source: The female mice with enhanced adult-born neurons also showed less neuronal loss of hilar mossy cells and hilar somatostatin-expressing neurons than wild-type females or males, which is notable because loss of these two hilar cell types is implicated in epileptogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical quantification data in Figure 7.

claim: Loss of hilar mossy cells and somatostatin-expressing neurons is implicated in epileptogenesis.
source: The female mice with enhanced adult-born neurons also showed less neuronal loss of hilar mossy cells and hilar somatostatin-expressing neurons than wild-type females or males, which is notable because loss of these two hilar cell types is implicated in epileptogenesis.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and citations in the epilepsy literature.

claim: Selective Bax deletion to increase adult-born neurons can reduce experimental epilepsy.
source: The results suggest that selective Bax deletion to increase adult-born neurons can reduce experimental epilepsy, and the effect shows a striking sex difference.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The effect of Bax deletion on epilepsy shows a striking sex difference.
source: The results suggest that selective Bax deletion to increase adult-born neurons can reduce experimental epilepsy, and the effect shows a striking sex difference.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analyses showing significant effects primarily in females.

claim: Past studies showed that suppressing adult-born neurons can also reduce chronic seizures.
source: The results are surprising in light of past studies showing that suppressing adult-born neurons can also reduce chronic seizures.
evidence: This references prior published work (Cho et al., 2015) showing opposite manipulations can have similar effects.

claim: Adult-born neurons are born in the subgranular zone (SGZ) of the dentate gyrus.
source: In the DG, adult-born neurons are born in the subgranular zone (SGZ; Altman and Das, 1965; Kaplan and Hinds, 1977; Altman, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple historical citations.

claim: Upon maturation, newborn neurons migrate to the granule cell layer (GCL).
source: Upon maturation, newborn neurons migrate to the granule cell layer (GCL; Cameron et al., 1993), develop almost exclusively into GCs, and integrate into the DG circuitry like other GCs (Ramirez-Amaya et al., 2006; Kempermann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited research on adult neurogenesis.

claim: Newborn neurons develop almost exclusively into granule cells (GCs).
source: Upon maturation, newborn neurons migrate to the granule cell layer (GCL; Cameron et al., 1993), develop almost exclusively into GCs, and integrate into the DG circuitry like other GCs (Ramirez-Amaya et al., 2006; Kempermann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited research on adult neurogenesis.

claim: Immature adult-born GCs can inhibit other GCs.
source: Prior studies suggest that the immature adult-born GCs can inhibit the other GCs (Ash et al., 2023) especially when they are up to 6-weeks-old (Drew et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited research on the functional properties of immature neurons.

claim: Immature adult-born GCs especially inhibit other GCs when they are up to 6-weeks-old.
source: Prior studies suggest that the immature adult-born GCs can inhibit the other GCs (Ash et al., 2023) especially when they are up to 6-weeks-old (Drew et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a specific citation (Drew et al., 2016).

claim: Young adult-born GCs support DG functions that require GCs to restrict action potential discharge, such as pattern separation.
source: By inhibition of the GC population, young adult-born GCs could support DG functions that require GCs to restrict action potential (AP) discharge, such as pattern separation (Sahay et al., 2011a; Sahay et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited research linking inhibition to pattern separation.

claim: Suppressing adult neurogenesis in mice appears to weaken pattern separation.
source: Indeed suppressing adult neurogenesis in mice appears to weaken pattern separation (Clelland et al., 2009; Nakashiba et al., 2012; Niibori et al., 2012; Tronel et al., 2012) and increasing adult neurogenesis improves it (Sahay et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Increasing adult neurogenesis improves pattern separation.
source: Indeed suppressing adult neurogenesis in mice appears to weaken pattern separation (Clelland et al., 2009; Nakashiba et al., 2012; Niibori et al., 2012; Tronel et al., 2012) and increasing adult neurogenesis improves it (Sahay et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sahay et al., 2011b.

claim: Strong excitation of GCs can cause excitotoxicity of hilar neurons, area CA1 pyramidal cells, and area CA3 pyramidal cells.
source: Thus, strong excitation of GCs can cause excitotoxicity of hilar neurons, area CA1 pyramidal cells, and area CA3 pyramidal cells (Scharfman and Schwartzkroin, 1990a; Scharfman and Schwartzkroin, 1990b; Sloviter, 1994; Scharfman, 1999; Sloviter et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research on excitotoxicity.

claim: Increasing adult-born neurons protects hilar neurons and CA3 from neuronal loss 3 days after severe seizures induced by pilocarpine.
source: Indeed, increasing adult-born neurons protects hilar neurons, and CA3 from neuronal loss 3 days after severe seizures are induced by the convulsant pilocarpine (Jain et al., 2019).
evidence: This references prior work by the authors (Jain et al., 2019).

claim: Status epilepticus (SE) is characterized by severe, continuous seizures lasting several hours.
source: The seizures induced by kainic acid or pilocarpine are severe, continuous, and last several hours, a condition called status epilepticus (SE).
evidence: This is a standard definition in epilepsy research.

claim: Neuronal injury in the hippocampus after SE is typically followed by chronic seizures (epilepsy) in rodents and humans.
source: The neuronal injury in the hippocampus after SE has been suggested to be important because it is typically followed by chronic seizures (epilepsy) in rodents and humans, and has been suggested to cause the epilepsy (Falconer et al., 1964; Sloviter, 1994; Cavalheiro et al., 1996; Herman, 2002; Mathern et al., 2008; Dudek and Staley, 2012; Dingledine et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to epilepsy research.

claim: Hippocampal neuronal injury after SE has been suggested to cause epilepsy.
source: The neuronal injury in the hippocampus after SE has been suggested to be important because it is typically followed by chronic seizures (epilepsy) in rodents and humans, and has been suggested to cause the epilepsy (Falconer et al., 1964; Sloviter, 1994; Cavalheiro et al., 1996; Herman, 2002; Mathern et al., 2008; Dudek and Staley, 2012; Dingledine et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by multiple citations.

claim: Chronic seizures after pilocarpine-induced SE involve the temporal lobe.
source: Chronic seizures involve the temporal lobe, so the type of epilepsy is called temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the pilocarpine model.

claim: After pilocarpine injection, spontaneous intermittent seizures begin several weeks later and continue for the lifespan.
source: Several weeks later, spontaneous intermittent seizures begin and continue for the lifespan (Scorza et al., 2009; Botterill et al., 2019; Lévesque et al., 2021; Whitebirch et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the pilocarpine model.

claim: SE increases adult neurogenesis.
source: It is known that SE increases adult neurogenesis (Parent and Kron, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: SE triggers a proliferation of progenitors in the week after SE.
source: SE triggers a proliferation of progenitors in the week after SE (Parent et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Parent et al., 1997.

claim: Many GCs that are born in the days after SE die in subsequent weeks by apoptosis.
source: Although many GCs that are born in the days after SE die in subsequent weeks by apoptosis, some survive.
evidence: This is established knowledge about post-SE neurogenesis.

claim: Young neurons that arise after SE and migrate into the GCL may suppress seizures by supporting the inhibition of GCs.
source: Young neurons that arise after SE and migrate into the GCL may suppress seizures by supporting the inhibition of GCs because adult-born GCs in the normal brain inhibit GCs when they are young (Drew et al., 2016; Ash et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on cited research about young neuron function.

claim: Newborn GCs in the GCL after SE can exhibit low excitability.
source: In addition, after SE, the newborn GCs in the GCL can exhibit low excitability (Jakubs et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jakubs et al., 2006.

claim: Some neurons born after SE mismigrate to ectopic locations such as the hilus (hilar ectopic GCs).
source: However, some neurons born after SE mismigrate to ectopic locations such as the hilus (hilar ectopic GCs), where they can contribute to recurrent excitatory circuits that promote seizures (Scharfman et al., 2000; Parent and Lowenstein, 2002; Scharfman, 2004; Scharfman and Hen, 2007b; Parent and Murphy, 2008; Scharfman and McCloskey, 2009; Zhan et al., 2010; Myers et al., 2013; Cho et al., 2015; Althaus et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to prior research.

claim: Hilar ectopic GCs can contribute to recurrent excitatory circuits that promote seizures.
source: However, some neurons born after SE mismigrate to ectopic locations such as the hilus (hilar ectopic GCs), where they can contribute to recurrent excitatory circuits that promote seizures (Scharfman et al., 2000; Parent and Lowenstein, 2002; Scharfman, 2004; Scharfman and Hen, 2007b; Parent and Murphy, 2008; Scharfman and McCloskey, 2009; Zhan et al., 2010; Myers et al., 2013; Cho et al., 2015; Althaus et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to prior research.

claim: Mossy cells are a major subset of glutamatergic hilar neurons which are vulnerable to excitotoxicity after SE.
source: Mossy cells are a major subset of glutamatergic hilar neurons which are vulnerable to excitotoxicity after SE (Scharfman, 1999; Sloviter et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: During SE, mossy cells may contribute to the activity that ultimately leads to widespread neuronal loss.
source: During SE, mossy cells may contribute to the activity that ultimately leads to widespread neuronal loss (Botterill et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: Surviving mossy cells can be beneficial after SE because they inhibit spontaneous chronic seizures in mice.
source: However, surviving mossy cells can be beneficial after SE because they inhibit spontaneous chronic seizures in mice (Bui et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bui et al., 2018.

claim: A large subset of vulnerable hilar neurons co-express GABA and somatostatin (SOM).
source: Another large subset of vulnerable hilar neurons co-express GABA and somatostatin (SOM; Sloviter, 1987; de Lanerolle et al., 1989; Freund et al., 1992; Sun et al., 2007) and correspond to so-called HIPP cells (neurons with hilar cell bodies and axons that project to the terminal zone of the perforant path; Han et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing these neurons.

claim: HIPP cells normally inhibit GCs and have the potential to prevent seizures.
source: HIPP cells are important because they normally inhibit GCs and have the potential to prevent seizures.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about HIPP cell function.

claim: The preservation of hilar mossy cells and SOM cells was found in females primarily.
source: Remarkably, the preservation of hilar mossy cells and SOM cells, and the reduction in chronic seizures, was found in females primarily.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analyses showing significant effects in females but not males.

claim: The sex difference may have been due to a greater ability to increase adult-born neurons in females than males.
source: The sex difference may have been due to a greater ability to increase adult-born neurons in females than males, consistent with sex differences in Bax- and caspase-dependent cell death (Forger et al., 2004; Siegel and McCullough, 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on observed data and cited literature on sex differences in cell death.

claim: Both increasing and suppressing adult-born neurons appear to reduce chronic seizures.
source: Therefore, taken together with the results presented here, both increasing and suppressing adult-born neurons appear to reduce chronic seizures.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the current findings with prior literature.

claim: Suppressing adult-born neurons led to a reduction in chronic seizures because there were fewer hilar ectopic granule cells.
source: Past studies suggested that suppressing adult-born neurons led to a reduction in chronic seizures because there were fewer hilar ectopic granule cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of prior research findings.

claim: Cre+ mice had a shorter duration of SE than Cre- mice.
source: The duration of SE was shorter in Cre+ mice compared to Cre- mice (Cre-: 280.5±14.6 min, n=11; Cre+: 211.4±17.2 min, n=14; Student's t-test, t(23)=0.30, p=0.007; Figure 1E2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative EEG data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1E2.

claim: The latency to the onset of the first seizure after pilocarpine injection was similar in Cre- and Cre+ mice.
source: When mice with and without electrodes were pooled, the latency to the onset of first seizure was similar in both genotypes (Cre-: 47.2±4.8 min, n=27; Cre+: 45.3±3.9 min, n=28; Student's t-test, t(53)=0.3, p=0.761; Figure 1D1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D1.

claim: Cre+ females had a shorter latency to the first seizure than Cre+ males.
source: Thus, a two-way ANOVA with genotype (Cre- and Cre+) and sex (female and male) as main factors showed a main effect of sex (F(1,51)=4.31; p=0.043) with Cre+ females exhibiting a shorter latency compared to Cre+ males (Cre+ females, 34.3±3.4 min, n=15; Cre+ males, 57.9±5.6 min, n=13; Tukey's post-hoc test, p=0.026) but not other groups (Cre- female, 46.7±9.3 min, n=12; Cre- males, 47.4±4.4 min, n=15; all p>0.344; Figure 1D3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of latency data shown in Figure 1D3.

claim: The total number of chronic seizures were similar in Cre- and Cre+ mice when sexes were pooled.
source: First, we analyzed data with sexes pooled (Figure 2C) and the total number of chronic seizures were similar in the two genotypes (Cre-: 22.6±3.0 seizures, n=18; Cre+: 21.3±1.6 seizures, n=17; Student's t-test, t(33)=0.15, p=0.882; Figure 2C1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative seizure data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C1.

claim: Cre+ females had approximately half the chronic seizures of Cre- females.
source: Tukey's post-hoc tests showed that Cre+ females had ~half the chronic seizures of Cre- females (Cre- female: 44.6±10.2 seizures, n=7; Cre+ female: 22.6±2.0 seizures, n=9; p=0.004; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative seizure data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C2.

claim: Cre+ males and Cre- males had a similar number of chronic seizures.
source: However, Cre+ males and Cre- males had a similar number of chronic seizures (Cre- male: 16.1±1.6 seizures, n=12; Cre+ male: 19.9±2.7 seizures, n=8; p>0.999; Figure 2C2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative seizure data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C2.

claim: Cre+ female mice had approximately half the seizures per day as Cre- females.
source: Cre+ female mice had approximately half the seizures per day as Cre- females (Tukey's post-hoc test, Cre- female: 2.1±0.5 seizures/day; Cre+ female: 1.1±0.1 seizures/day; p=0.004; Figure 2D2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative seizure frequency data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D2.

claim: Female seizure durations were shorter than male seizure durations.
source: When separated by sex, a two-way ANOVA showed that female seizure durations were shorter than males (F(1,29)=12.42; p=0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of seizure duration data.

claim: Cre+ females had longer seizure durations than Cre- females when all seizures were analyzed.
source: Post-hoc tests showed that Cre+ females had longer seizure durations than Cre- females (Cre- female: 33.2±0.7 s; Cre+ female: 39.3±0.6 s, p<0.001; Figure 2F2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative seizure duration data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F2.

claim: Males had little evidence of postictal depression but it was common in females.
source: We found that males had little evidence of postictal depression but it was common in females (Figure 3), a sex difference that is consistent with greater spreading depolarization in females (Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2009; Bolay et al., 2011; Kudo et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by EEG analysis data shown in Figure 3 and citations to prior research on sex differences in spreading depolarization.

claim: The number and percentages of seizures with postictal depression were reduced in Cre+ females compared to Cre- females.
source: When all chronic seizures were analyzed (n=274), the number and percentages of seizures with postictal depression were reduced in Cre+ females compared to Cre- females (Fisher's exact test, p=0.009; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of postictal depression shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All females showed more postictal depression than all males.
source: There was a sex difference, with all females showing more postictal depression (108/154 seizures, 70.5%) than all males (17/120 seizures, 14.2%; Fisher's exact tests, p<0.0001, Figure 3B-C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Cre+ females had fewer days with ≥3 seizures than Cre- females.
source: Cre+ females had fewer days with ≥3 seizures than Cre- females (Cre- females: 6.3±1.4 days; Cre+ females: 3.0±0.4 days; Tukey's post-hoc test, p=0.009; Figure 4D3).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of seizure clustering shown in Figure 4D3.

claim: Cre+ mice had more DCX than Cre- mice immediately before SE.
source: A two-way ANOVA with sex and genotype as factors showed a significant effect of genotype (F(1,9)=60.78, p<0.001) but not sex (F(1,9)=1.20, p=0.301; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative DCX immunoreactivity data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Cre+ females had more DCX than Cre- females before SE.
source: Post-hoc comparisons showed that Cre+ females had more DCX than Cre- females (p=0.001) and the same was true for males (p=0.003).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DCX data.

claim: The area fraction of DCX in the GCL/SGZ was significantly greater in Cre+ mice than Cre- mice after chronic seizures had developed.
source: Representative examples of DCX expression in the GCL/SGZ are presented in Figure 5F and Figure 5E shows the area fraction of DCX in the GCL/SGZ was significantly greater in Cre+ mice than Cre- mice (Cre-: 3.1±0.4%, n=20; Cre+: 4.2±0.3%, n=17; Student's t-test, t(35)=2.13, p=0.041; Figure 5D1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative DCX data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: Cre+ females had more DCX than Cre- females after chronic seizures had developed.
source: There was a significant effect of genotype (F(1,33)=12.62, p=0.001) and sex (F(1,33)=11.68, p=0.002), with Cre+ females having more DCX than Cre- females (Cre- female: 1.8±0.3, n=7; Cre+ female: 3.8±0.4, n=9; Tukey's post-hoc test, p=0.015; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative DCX data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: DCX levels were similar between Cre+ and Cre- male mice after chronic seizures had developed.
source: In contrast, DCX levels were similar between Cre+ and Cre- male mice (p=0.498, Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DCX data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Cre+ mice had significantly more hilar Prox1 cells than Cre- mice.
source: Cre+ mice had significantly more hilar Prox1 cells than Cre- mice (Cre-: 19.6±1.9 cells, n=18; Cre+: 60.5±7.9 cells, n=18; Student's t-test, t(34)=5.76, p<0.001; Figure 6C1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative Prox1 cell counts shown in Figure 6C1.

claim: Cre+ mice had more GluR2/3-expressing hilar cells than Cre- mice.
source: The results showed that Cre+ mice had more GluR2/3-expressing hilar cells than Cre- mice (Cre-: 10.0±1.8 cells, n=10; Cre+: 17.0±2.0 cells, n=13; Student's t-test, t(21)=2.46, p=0.022; Fig. 7A1-3).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative GluR2/3 cell counts shown in Figure 7A3.

claim: Cre+ females had more GluR2/3 cells than Cre- females.
source: There was a significant effect of genotype (F(1,18)=4.95, p=0.039) with Cre+ females having more GluR2/3 cells than Cre- females (Cre- female: 8.0±2.0 cells, n=6; Cre+ female: 19.1±2.7 cells, n=8; Tukey's post-hoc test, p=0.011; Figure 7A4).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative GluR2/3 cell counts and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7A4.

claim: GluR2/3-ir hilar cells were similar in Cre+ and Cre- males.
source: GluR2/3-ir hilar cells were similar in males (Cre- male: 13.0±3.0 cells, n=4; Cre+ male: 13.6±2.5 cells, n=5; p=0.915; Figure 7A4).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative GluR2/3 cell counts and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7A4.

claim: Cre+ mice had more hilar SOM cells than Cre- mice.
source: Next, we measured SOM hilar cells in pooled data (females and males together). These results were analogous to the data for GluR2/3, showing that Cre+ mice had more hilar SOM cells than Cre- mice (Cre-: 2.1±0.5 cells, n=9; Cre+: 4.6±0.6 cells, n=11; Student's t-test, t(18)=2.95, p=0.008; Fig. 7B1-3).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative SOM cell counts shown in Figure 7B3.

claim: Cre+ females had more SOM cells than Cre- females.
source: However, Cre+ females had more SOM cells than Cre- females (Cre- female: 2.2±0.6 cells, n=6; Cre+ female: 5.1±0.6 cells, n=8; Tukey's post-hoc test, p=0.019; Figure 7B4), although only in dorsal DG (Figure 7B4) not ventral DG (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative SOM cell counts and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B4.

claim: Numbers of SOM cells were similar in Cre+ and Cre- males.
source: Numbers of SOM cells were similar in males (Cre- male: 2.2±0.7 cells, n=3; Cre+ male: 3.3±1.8 cells, n=3; p=0.897; Figure 7B4) in both dorsal and ventral DG (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative SOM cell counts and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B4.

claim: Parvalbumin-ir cells were not significantly different between Cre+ and Cre- genotypes.
source: Parvalbumin-ir cells were not significantly different between genotypes (Student's test, t(19)=1.76, p=0.095; Fig. 7C1-3).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative parvalbumin cell counts shown in Figure 7C3.

claim: Cre+ female mice had less Fluorojade C staining in the subiculum than Cre- female mice.
source: For females, a two-way ANOVA with genotype and subfield as factors showed a significant effect of genotype (F(1,14)=11.21, p=0.005) with a smaller area fraction in Cre+ mice than Cre- mice for subiculum (p=0.032) and a trend in CA1 (p=0.060; Figure 8D1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative Fluorojade C data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 8D1.

claim: Males showed no significant differences in Fluorojade C staining between genotypes.
source: Males showed no significant differences either in genotype (F(1,8)=0.02, p=0.872) or subfield (F(1,8)=0.16, p=0.698; Figure 8D2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative Fluorojade C data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 8D2.

claim: The incidence of SE was significantly higher in unimplanted mice compared to implanted mice.
source: The incidence of SE was significantly higher in the unimplanted mice when sexes and genotypes were pooled (Fisher's exact test, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Genotype had no effect on the incidence of SE.
source: Genotype had no effect on the incidence of SE (Unimplanted, p>0.999; Implanted, p=0.565).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of SE incidence data.

claim: The total number of chronic seizures and seizure frequency were similar in implanted and unimplanted mice.
source: The total number of chronic seizures (F(1,17)=1.33, p=0.265) and seizure frequency (F(1,17)=1.27, p=0.276) were similar, suggesting that implantation did not influence chronic seizures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There were no significant differences in mortality associated with SE or chronic seizures between groups.
source: There were no significant differences in mortality associated with SE or chronic seizures. For quantification, we examined mortality during SE and the subsequent 3 days, 3 days until the end of the 3-week-long-EEG recording period, or both (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A). Graphs of mouse numbers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B1) or percentages of mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B2) were similar: groups (Cre- females, Cre+ females, Cre- males, Cre+ males) were not significantly different (Fisher's exact tests, all p >0.05).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mortality data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Power during SE showed no effect of genotype for any frequency range.
source: Two-way RMANOVA with genotype and time as main factors showed no effect of genotype for any frequency range: delta (1–4 Hz, F(1,7)=1.61; p=0.245); theta (4–8 Hz, F(1,7)=1.75; p=0.227); beta (8–30 Hz, F(1,7)=1.65; p=0.240); low gamma (80 Hz, F(1,7)=0.29; p=0.174); high gamma (80–100 Hz, F(1,7)=0.17; p=0.689).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of power spectral data.

claim: There was a significant effect of time on power for all frequency bands during SE.
source: There was a significant effect of time for all bands (delta, p=0.003; theta, p=0.002, beta, low gamma, and high gamma, p<0.001), which is consistent with the declining power in SE with time.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of power spectral data over time.

claim: The timing of SE was not significantly different in females than in males.
source: However, the timing of SE was not significantly different in females than in males (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative timing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Postictal depression is often associated with spreading depolarization.
source: In recent years the advent of DC amplifiers made it possible to show that postictal depression is often associated with spreading depolarization (Ssentongo et al., 2017), a large depolarization shift that is accompanied by depolarization block.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ssentongo et al., 2017.

claim: The sex difference in postictal depression is consistent with greater spreading depolarization in females.
source: We found that males had little evidence of postictal depression but it was common in females (Figure 3), a sex difference that is consistent with greater spreading depolarization in females (Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2009; Bolay et al., 2011; Kudo et al., 2023).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to prior research on sex differences in spreading depolarization.

claim: The shorter female seizures may have been due to truncation of seizures by spreading depolarization.
source: Because females exhibited more postictal depression (see Figure 3), corresponding to spreading depolarization (Ssentongo et al., 2017), the shorter female seizures may have been due to truncation of seizures by spreading depolarization.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed data and cited literature.

claim: Cre+ females may have had longer seizures because they were protected from spreading depolarization.
source: Cre+ females may have had longer seizures because they were protected from spreading depolarization.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed data on seizure duration and postictal depression.

claim: Clusters of seizures can have a substantial impact on the quality of life.
source: Clustering is commonly manifested in consecutive days with frequent seizures. Clusters of seizures can have a substantial impact on the quality of life (Haut, 2015; Jafarpour et al., 2019) so they are important.
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical research on seizure clusters.

claim: In humans, clusters are defined as at least 3 seizures within 24 hr.
source: In humans, clusters are defined as at least 3 seizures within 24 hr (Goffin et al., 2007; Jafarpour et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical definitions.

claim: Prox1 is a common marker of GCs in the GCL.
source: Prox1 is a common marker of GCs in the GCL (Pleasure et al., 2000; Galeeva et al., 2007; Galichet et al., 2008; Steiner et al., 2008; Iwano et al., 2012), and the hilus (Scharfman et al., 2007a; Hester and Danzer, 2013; Cho et al., 2015; Bermudez-Hernandez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing Prox1 as a marker.

claim: In past studies, hilar ectopic GCs have been suggested to promote seizures.
source: In past studies, hilar ectopic GCs have been suggested to promote seizures (Scharfman et al., 2000; Jung et al., 2006; Cho et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There was a correlation between the number of hilar ectopic GCs and the number of chronic seizures in Cre- mice, suggesting more hilar ectopic GCs improved rather than worsened seizures.
source: When Cre- and Cre+ mice were compared (both sexes pooled), there was a correlation with number of chronic seizures (Figure 6D1) but it suggested that more hilar ectopic GCs improved rather than worsened seizures. However, the correlation was only in Cre- mice, and when sexes were separated there was no correlation (Figure 6D3).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 6D1 and 6D3.

claim: Hilar ectopic granule cells had no consistent effect on chronic seizures.
source: In light of these inconsistent results, it seems that hilar ectopic granule cells had no consistent effect on chronic seizures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inconsistent correlation data.

claim: Epileptogenesis after a brain insult like SE is suggested to be due to the hippocampal damage caused by the insult.
source: It has been suggested that epileptogenesis after a brain insult like SE is due to the hippocampal damage caused by the insult (Cavalheiro et al., 1996; Herman, 2002; Mathern et al., 2008; Dudek and Staley, 2012; Dingledine et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by multiple citations.

claim: Loss of hilar mossy cells and SOM cells has been suggested to be critical for epileptogenesis.
source: Here, we examined the loss of vulnerable hilar mossy cells and SOM cells because they have been suggested to be critical (Sloviter, 1987; Cavazos and Sutula, 1990; Cavazos et al., 1994; Henshall and Meldrum, 2012; Huusko et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: An antibody to GluR2/3 was used as a marker of mossy cells.
source: An antibody to GluR2/3 was used as a marker of mossy cells (Leranth et al., 1996) and a SOM antibody for SOM cells (Leranth et al., 1990; Savanthrapadian et al., 2014; Botterill et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing the use of these markers.

claim: GluR2/3+ hilar cells were not double-labeled with Prox1, suggesting they corresponded to mossy cells, not hilar ectopic GCs.
source: We confirmed that the GluR2/3+ hilar cells were not double-labeled with Prox1, suggesting they corresponded to mossy cells, not hilar ectopic GCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by double-labeling data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Having more GluR2/3-ir mossy cells could be a mechanism that allowed Cre+ females to have reduced chronic seizures compared to Cre- females.
source: These results in dorsal DG also were obtained in ventral DG (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-C). The data suggest that having more GluR2/3-ir mossy cells could be a mechanism that allowed Cre+ females to have reduced chronic seizures compared to Cre- females.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed preservation of mossy cells in Cre+ females.

claim: Equal numbers of GluR2/3 mossy cells in Cre+ and Cre- males could relate to their lack of protection against chronic seizures.
source: Equal numbers of GluR2/3 mossy cells in Cre+ and Cre- males could relate to their lack of protection against chronic seizures.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed lack of difference in males.

claim: The ability to preserve more mossy cells and SOM hilar cells in Cre+ females could be a mechanism by which Cre+ females were protected from chronic seizures.
source: Therefore, the ability to preserve more mossy cells and SOM hilar cells in Cre+ females could be a mechanism by which Cre+ females were protected from chronic seizures.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed preservation of these cell types in Cre+ females.

claim: Loss of parvalbumin-expressing cells has not been considered to play a substantial role in epileptogenesis in the past.
source: These data are consistent with the idea that loss of parvalbumin-expressing cells has not been considered to play a substantial in epileptogenesis in the past (Sloviter, 1987; Sloviter, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Parvalbumin expression may decline even if the cells do not die.
source: However, it should be noted that subsequent research has shown that the topic is complicated because parvalbumin expression may decline even if the cells do not die (André et al., 2001; Sun et al., 2007) and data vary depending on the animal model (van Vliet et al., 2004; Huusko et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to subsequent research.

claim: Prior studies showed hilar and CA3 neurons are protected from cell loss in Cre+ mice examined 3 days after SE.
source: In our previous study of Cre+ and Cre- mice (Jain et al., 2019), tamoxifen was administered at 6 weeks and SE was induced at 12 weeks (like the current study). We examined neuronal loss 3 days after SE, when neuronal loss in the hilus and area CA3 is robust in wild-type mice. There is also some neuronal loss in CA1 at 3 days but more at 10 days after SE. We found less neuronal loss in Cre+ mice in these three areas (Jain et al., 2019).
evidence: This references prior work by the authors (Jain et al., 2019).

claim: Delayed cell death occurs in CA1 and the subiculum at 10 days after SE.
source: In the current study, we examined 10 days after SE (Figure 8A–B) because at this time delayed neuronal loss occurs, providing a better understanding of CA1 and the subiculum because delayed cell death occurs there.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the time course of cell death after SE.

claim: Cre+ female mice were protected from damage in CA1 and subiculum relative to Cre- females.
source: Thus, Cre+ female mice were protected from damage relative to Cre- females.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on Fluorojade C staining data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Increasing young adult-born neurons before the epileptogenic insult can protect against epilepsy.
source: This study showed that conditional deletion of Bax from Nestin-expressing progenitors increased young adult-born neurons in the DG when studied 6 weeks after deletion and using DCX as a marker of immature neurons. In a different set of mice, pilocarpine was used to induce epileptogenesis. The chronic seizures, measured 4–7 weeks after pilocarpine, were reduced in frequency by about 50% in females. Therefore, increasing young adult-born neurons before the epileptogenic insult can protect against epilepsy.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental data.

claim: We do not know if the protective effect was due to the greater number of new neurons before SE or other effects.
source: However, we do not know if the protective effect was due to the greater number of new neurons before SE or other effects.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in interpreting the mechanism.

claim: Increased numbers of newborn neurons before SE likely lead to a reduced SE duration and less neuronal damage in the days after SE.
source: Past data would suggest that increased numbers of newborn neurons before SE lead to a reduced SE duration and less neuronal damage in the days after SE (Jain et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on prior published work.

claim: Reduced neuronal damage after SE would be likely to lessen the epilepsy after SE.
source: That would be likely to lessen the epilepsy after SE.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the hypothesis that neuronal damage causes epilepsy.

claim: There may have been additional effects of larger numbers of newborn neurons prior to SE beyond reduced SE duration and neuronal damage.
source: However, there may have been additional effects of larger numbers of newborn neurons prior to SE.
evidence: This acknowledges that other mechanisms may contribute.

claim: By protecting against SE-induced neuronal loss, young adult-born neurons could have reduced the severity of epilepsy.
source: Increasing young adult-born neurons has been shown to protect the hippocampus from SE-induced neuronal loss (Jain et al., 2019) which is a major contributor to epileptogenesis. Therefore, by protecting against SE-induced neuronal loss the young adult-born neurons could have reduced the severity of epilepsy.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed neuroprotection and cited literature.

claim: The results are unexpected because suppressing adult-born neurons was shown to reduce chronic seizures.
source: First, the results are unexpected because suppressing adult-born neurons was shown to reduce chronic seizures (Cho et al., 2015). Here, increasing adult-born neurons did not have the opposite effect.
evidence: This highlights the surprising nature of the findings in light of prior research.

claim: The larger effect of increasing adult-born neurons in female mice may be attributable to sex differences in Bax.
source: The larger effect of increasing adult-born neurons in female mice may be attributable to sex differences in Bax (discussed below).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed sex differences and literature on Bax.

claim: The association of more hilar ectopic GCs with fewer chronic seizures was unexpected.
source: The association of more hilar ectopic GCs with fewer chronic seizures was unexpected.
evidence: This highlights the surprising nature of the hilar ectopic GC findings.

claim: SE might have been less severe in the Cre+ females, and this could have contributed to reduced neuronal loss and chronic seizures.
source: In the Cre+ females, however, it was unclear. Nevertheless, the first seizure after pilocarpine injection was often less severe in Cre+ females, and power showed a tendency to be reduced during SE. Therefore, SE might have been less severe in the Cre+ females, and this could have contributed to reduced neuronal loss and chronic seizures.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed SE characteristics in Cre+ females.

claim: It is remarkable that increasing adult-born neurons for 6 weeks was sufficient to reduce seizures long-term.
source: It is remarkable that increasing adult-born neurons for 6 weeks was sufficient to reduce seizures long-term.
evidence: This is a commentary on the significance of the findings.

claim: Normally the young adult-born neurons inhibit other GCs, which supports the DG gate function.
source: It is consistent with the idea that normally the young adult-born neurons inhibit other GCs, which supports the DG gate function (Hsu, 2007; Drew et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited literature about DG function.

claim: The DG gate has been suggested to be an inhibitory barrier to entry of seizures from cortex into hippocampus.
source: This gate has been suggested to be an inhibitory barrier to entry of seizures from cortex into hippocampus (Coulter and Carlson, 2007; Hsu, 2007; Krook-Magnuson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on the DG gate.

claim: Seizures that pass from entorhinal cortex to the GCs and then CA3 are likely to continue to CA1 and back to cortex, causing reverberatory (long-lasting, severe) seizures.
source: That entry is deleterious because seizures that pass from entorhinal cortex to the GCs and then CA3 are likely to continue to CA1 and back to cortex, causing reverberatory (long-lasting, severe) seizures.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about hippocampal circuitry and seizure propagation.

claim: The GCs have especially powerful excitatory synapses on CA3 pyramidal cells.
source: Also, the GCs have especially powerful excitatory synapses on CA3 pyramidal cells (Henze et al., 2000; Scharfman and MacLusky, 2014), although these are normally mitigated by GABAergic circuitry (Acsády et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on hippocampal synapses.

claim: Adult-born neurons protect against other pathological conditions such as Alzheimer's disease.
source: These data are consistent with the demonstration that adult-born neurons protect against other pathological conditions such as Alzheimer's disease (Choi et al., 2018; Choi and Tanzi, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on adult neurogenesis and Alzheimer's disease.

claim: All effects are unlikely to be mediated only by the DG.
source: However, it is important to note that all effects are unlikely to be mediated only by the DG. The olfactory bulb and other areas also have adult-born neurons and they could contribute to epilepsy, especially those epilepsy syndromes with mechanisms that are extrahippocampal.
evidence: This acknowledges that other brain regions with adult neurogenesis may contribute.

claim: The results may have underestimated the effect on clusters because the interval between clusters increased in some mice so they only had one cluster in 3 weeks.
source: The results may have underestimated the effect on clusters because we did not measure the interval between clusters in many Cre+ female mice. The reason is that the interval between clusters increased in some mice so they only had one cluster in 3 weeks. Thus intercluster interval appeared to lengthen in Cre+ females but animals with only one cluster had to be excluded. In the end, the results were not statistically significant.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the limitations in measuring intercluster intervals.

claim: Before SE, there was no sex difference in DCX levels between Cre+ females and Cre+ males.
source: Insight into this sex difference came when the same assessments were made before SE because at that time there was no sex difference. Cre+ females had more adult-born neurons than Cre- females and Cre+ males had more than Cre- males. In addition, the levels of DCX were similar in Cre+ females and Cre+ males.
evidence: This is based on DCX quantification data before SE.

claim: After epilepsy developed, Cre- females had less DCX than Cre- males.
source: However, after epilepsy developed, there was a sex difference. Cre- females had less DCX than Cre-males.
evidence: This is based on DCX quantification data after epilepsy developed.

claim: Cell birth during epileptogenesis may have been greater in males because it is in the developing hippocampus.
source: One explanation is that cell birth during epileptogenesis was greater in males because it is in the developing hippocampus (Sisk et al., 2016) and SE has been suggested to rekindle developmental programs (Ben-Ari and Holmes, 2006).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on cited literature.

claim: Males may have had less programmed cell death during epileptogenesis.
source: Another possibility is males had less programmed cell death during epileptogenesis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the sex difference.

claim: During development, females have more apoptotic profiles than males and the sex difference was blocked by Bax deletion.
source: Indeed during development, females have more apoptotic profiles than males and the sex difference was blocked by Bax deletion (Forger et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Forger et al., 2004.

claim: Cell death during epileptogenesis may be Bax-dependent in females but Bax-independent in males.
source: A final possibility is that cell death during epileptogenesis is Bax-dependent in females but Bax-independent in males. Support for this idea comes from studies of ischemic cell death, which is caspase-dependent in females but not males (Siegel and McCullough, 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation to research on sex differences in cell death mechanisms.

claim: In the normal brain, adult-born neurons in the DG are thought to arise mainly from the SGZ and migrate to the GCL.
source: In the normal brain, adult-born neurons in the DG are thought to arise mainly from the SGZ and migrate to the GCL (Kempermann, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kempermann, 2012.

claim: After SE, there is a surge in proliferation in the SGZ, and neurons either migrate correctly to the GCL or aberrantly in the hilus.
source: After SE, there is a surge in proliferation in the SGZ, and neurons either migrate correctly to the GCL or aberrantly in the hilus (Parent et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Parent et al., 1997.

claim: Hilar ectopic GCs are innervated by residual CA3 neurons, and project to GCs, making a major contribution to mossy fiber innervation of GCs in the inner molecular layer.
source: These hilar ectopic GCs are thought to contribute to seizure generation in the epileptic brain because they are innervated by residual CA3 neurons, and project to GCs, making a major contribution to mossy fiber innervation of GCs in the inner molecular layer (Scharfman et al., 2000; Kron et al., 2010; Pierce et al., 2011; Scharfman and Pierce, 2012; Althaus et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing hilar ectopic GC connectivity.

claim: When epileptiform activity occurs in CA3 in slices of epileptic rats, CA3 evokes discharges in hilar ectopic GCs that in turn excite GCs in the GCL.
source: When epileptiform activity occurs in CA3 in slices of epileptic rats, CA3 evokes discharges in hilar ectopic GCs that in turn excite GCs in the GCL (Scharfman et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Scharfman et al., 2000.

claim: The numbers of hilar ectopic GCs are correlated with chronic seizure frequency in rats and mice.
source: Consistent with the idea that hilar ectopic GCs promote seizures, the numbers of hilar ectopic GCs are correlated with chronic seizure frequency in rats (McCloskey et al., 2006) and mice (Hester and Danzer, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Suppressing hilar ectopic GC formation reduces chronic seizures.
source: Furthermore, suppressing hilar ectopic GC formation reduces chronic seizures (Jung et al., 2006; Cho et al., 2015; Hosford et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: This is the first study to show that increased hilar ectopic GCs were found in mice that had reduced seizures.
source: Notably, this is the first study to our knowledge showing that increased hilar ectopic GCs were found in mice that had reduced seizures.
evidence: This highlights the novelty of the finding.

claim: SE-induced hippocampal damage was reduced in Cre+ females with high numbers of hilar ectopic GCs.
source: One potential explanation is that SE-induced hippocampal damage was reduced in Cre+ females with high numbers of hilar ectopic GCs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the unexpected finding.

claim: The circuitry of the DG would be very different in Cre+ females compared to past studies of hilar ectopic GCs where neuronal loss was severe.
source: Therefore, the circuitry of the DG would be very different compared to past studies of hilar ectopic GCs where a neuronal loss was severe .
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed neuroprotection.

claim: The presence of mossy cells is one way the circuitry would be different.
source: The presence of mossy cells is one way the circuitry would be different. MCs normally support the young adult-born GCs that migrate to the GCL (Piatti and Schinder, 2018). Mossy cells provide an important activator of newborn GCs when they are young (Chancey et al., 2014). Mossy cells also innervate hilar ectopic GCs (Pierce et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited literature about mossy cell function.

claim: There was protection against chronic seizures in female Cre+ mice by increasing adult-born neurons in the GCL.
source: Another possibility is that there was protection against chronic seizures in female Cre+ mice by increasing adult-born neurons in the GCL. The reason to suggest this possibility is that prior studies showed that young adult-born neurons in the GCL primarily inhibit GCs in the normal brain (Drew et al., 2016) and are relatively quiescent in the epileptic brain (Jakubs et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on cited literature about adult-born neuron function.

claim: This study is limited by the possibilities of type II statistical errors in comparisons of 3–5 mice/group.
source: This study is limited by the possibilities of type II statistical errors in those instances where we divided groups by genotype and sex, leading to comparisons of 3–5 mice/group.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study.

claim: Female mice were selected regardless of the stage of the estrous cycle.
source: Another potential caveat is that female mice were selected regardless of the stage of the estrous cycle.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study.

claim: In the past, suppressing adult neurogenesis before SE was followed by fewer hilar ectopic GCs and reduced chronic seizures.
source: In the past, suppressing adult neurogenesis before SE was followed by fewer hilar ectopic GCs and reduced chronic seizures.
evidence: This summarizes prior research findings.

claim: Enhancing adult-born neurons before SE and increased hilar ectopic GCs does not necessarily reduce seizures.
source: Here, we show that the opposite - enhancing adult-born neurons before SE and increased hilar ectopic GCs - does not necessarily reduce seizures.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current findings.

claim: Protection of the hilar neurons from SE-induced excitotoxicity was critical to reducing seizures.
source: We suggest instead that protection of the hilar neurons from SE-induced excitotoxicity was critical to reducing seizures. The reason for the suggestion is that the survival of hilar neurons would lead to the persistence of the normal inhibitory functions of hilar neurons, protecting against seizures.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed neuroprotection and seizure reduction.

claim: The survival of hilar neurons would lead to the persistence of the normal inhibitory functions of hilar neurons, protecting against seizures.
source: The reason for the suggestion is that the survival of hilar neurons would lead to the persistence of the normal inhibitory functions of hilar neurons, protecting against seizures.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the mechanism of protection.

claim: We do not have data to prove that protection of hilar neurons was the mechanism for reducing seizures.
source: However, this is only a suggestion at the present time because we do not have data to prove it.
evidence: This acknowledges the speculative nature of the proposed mechanism.

claim: Sex differences are likely to have played an important role in the protective effects.
source: Additionally, because protection was in females, sex differences are likely to have played an important role.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed sex differences.

claim: Enhancing young adult-born neurons in Nestin-Cre+ mice had a striking effect in the pilocarpine model, reducing chronic seizures in female mice.
source: Regardless, the results show that enhancing-born neurons of young adult-born neurons in Nestin-Cre+ mice had a striking effect in the pilocarpine model, reducing chronic seizures in female mice.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.
